I am 50 years old this year, and I have been farming in Quzhou County since I was a young girl. My family has 4 mu of flat land, and every year I plant winter wheat in autumn and summer maize right after the wheat harvest. I only went to primary school, but I know these fields better than any book. I have watched my father, my husband, and now my own hands work this soil for over 30 years.

This year, I will stick to wheat and maize like always. They are the only crops I trust. The grain station buys wheat at a stable price, and there is always someone in the village who comes to collect maize for the feed mills. Two years ago, my neighbor Aunt Wang planted cotton and spent all her savings on picking labor — she ended up with nothing. I cannot take that risk. My family needs to eat, and my grandson needs money for school.

For wheat, I will sow in mid-October. I keep my own seed from last year — it is an improved variety called Jimai 22 that my brother gave me three years ago. I will hire the rotary tiller to prepare the land, then broadcast the seed. Before sowing, I will spread one 50 kg bag of compound fertilizer on each mu. The shop sells a brand that says 18-16-6 on the bag — the red one. When March comes and the wheat starts jointing, if the leaves look yellow, I will put down another half bag of urea per mu. I learned from my neighbor Li that if you skip the topdressing, the yield drops badly. I will irrigate three times: the winter irrigation before the freeze, the jointing water, and one more at grain filling. The electricity bill for pumping is getting expensive, so three times is what I can manage. For chemicals, I spray herbicide once in early spring for the weeds, insecticide once when the aphids come, and if the spring is rainy, maybe fungicide once. So three sprays in total.

For summer maize, there is no time to rest after wheat harvest in early June. I must plant within three or four days before the season slips away. I will buy hybrid maize seed from the village shop — whatever variety they have, usually Nongda something. I will not till the land again; there is no time, and everyone in our village now plants maize directly into the wheat stubble. At sowing, I put compound fertilizer in the holes, about 50 kg per mu. Then when the maize grows to knee height, I topdress with urea. I will irrigate twice: once right after sowing if the soil is dry, and once in July when the heat comes. For pests, herbicide once and insecticide once for the corn borers — two sprays total.

I expect about 500 kg of wheat per mu and around 550 kg of maize per mu. Last year was too dry and I only got 420 kg of wheat, but this winter the snow was good and the soil moisture looks better. I do not have much extra cash — my husband works part-time in town and sends some home, but we have to pay for our grandson's school. So I cannot buy the most expensive inputs. But I also know that if I cut too much on fertilizer, my family will go hungry. I follow what my neighbors do, and this plan has kept us fed for 30 years. That is enough reason for me.
